reason: The sources provide 16 verified claims across six independent sites regarding gravity at ISS altitude and the physiological effects of weightlessness.
story: Think you’ve escaped Earth’s pull on the International Space Station? Think again. While many believe space is a zero-G vacuum, the Earth’s gravitational field at the station's altitude is still nearly 90 percent as strong as it is on the ground. Astronauts don't float because gravity is gone; they float because they are in a state of perpetual free fall, plummeting toward the planet at high horizontal speeds that carry them around the curve of the Earth. This constant weightlessness takes a brutal toll on the human body. Fluid shifts toward the head, creating a puffy moon-face appearance, while muscles and bones begin to waste away. Some astronauts even experience squashed eyeballs that shift their vision toward farsightedness. From Gherman Titov’s first reported space sickness in 1961 to the Vomit Comet training flights, science proves that you can never truly run away from the gravity of home.
angle: At the altitude of the International Space Station, Earth’s gravity is still nearly 90 percent as strong as it is on the ground.

claims.claim: Earth's gravity at ISS altitude is nearly 90 percent of its strength on the ground.
Astronauts feel weightless because they are in a state of constant free fall.
Objects in orbit stay up by falling around or over the horizon of the Earth.
Satellites stay in space due to their high horizontal speed.
Gravity is a force that exists everywhere in the universe.
Normal gravity on Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 meters per second squared.
Space adaptation syndrome, or space sickness, affects roughly half of all astronauts.
Space sickness symptoms typically resolve within 72 hours.
Cosmonaut Gherman Titov reported the first case of space sickness in 1961.
Fluid shifts in space cause a puffy facial appearance known as moon-face.
Lack of weight-bearing in space leads to muscle atrophy and loss of strength.
Astronauts experience bone density loss called spaceflight osteopenia.
Parabolic flights on aircraft are used to simulate microgravity environments for training.
Some astronauts experience vision shifts or squashed eyeballs while in orbit.
An object at the exact center of the Earth would achieve a state of weightlessness.
NASA used twins Scott and Mark Kelly to compare spaceflight effects on the human body.

disputed: S1 states 45 percent of astronauts experience space sickness, while S4 says nearly half; the script should use nearly half.
S2 states gravity is nearly 90 percent as strong at orbital altitude, while S3 specifies 88.8 percent; use nearly 90 percent.
